claim: Torsional strain imposed by DNA-processing enzymes induces supercoiling of DNA, which triggers large structural rearrangements through the formation of plectonemes.
source: Torsional strain imposed by DNA-processing enzymes induces supercoiling of DNA, which triggers large structural rearrangements through the formation of plectonemes (Vinograd et al., 1965).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vinograd et al., 1965

claim: Supercoiling plays an important role in the regulation of gene expression in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: Recent biochemical studies suggest that supercoiling plays an important role in the regulation of gene expression in both prokaryotes (Le et al., 2013) and eukaryotes (Naughton et al., 2013; Pasi and Lavery, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Le et al., 2013; Naughton et al., 2013; Pasi and Lavery, 2016

claim: Chromatin is organized into independent topological domains with varying degrees of torsional strain.
source: In order to tailor the degree of supercoiling around specific genes, chromatin is organized into independent topological domains with varying degrees of torsional strain (Naughton et al., 2013; Sinden and Pettijohn, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Naughton et al., 2013; Sinden and Pettijohn, 1981

claim: Domains that contain highly transcribed genes are generally underwound whereas inactive genes are overwound.
source: Domains that contain highly transcribed genes are generally underwound whereas inactive genes are overwound (Kouzine et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kouzine et al., 2013

claim: Transcription of a gene transiently alters the local supercoiling.
source: Furthermore, transcription of a gene transiently alters the local supercoiling (Kouzine et al., 2013; Naughton et al., 2013; Peter et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kouzine et al., 2013; Naughton et al., 2013; Peter et al., 2004

claim: Torsional strain influences the rate of transcription.
source: while, in turn, torsional strain influences the rate of transcription (Chong et al., 2014; Liu and Wang, 1987; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chong et al., 2014; Liu and Wang, 1987; Ma et al., 2013

claim: Supercoiling has been acknowledged as a key component of the spatial architecture of the genome.
source: More recently, supercoiling has been acknowledged as a key component of the spatial architecture of the genome (de Wit and de Laat, 2012; Dekker et al., 2013; Ding et al., 2014; Neuman, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to de Wit and de Laat, 2012; Dekker et al., 2013; Ding et al., 2014; Neuman, 2010

claim: The DNA sequence influences its local mechanical properties such as bending stiffness, curvature, and duplex stability.
source: However, the DNA sequence influences its local mechanical properties such as bending stiffness, curvature, and duplex stability, which in turn alter the energetics of plectoneme formation at specific sequences (Dittmore et al., 2017; Irobalieva et al., 2015; Matek et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dittmore et al., 2017; Irobalieva et al., 2015; Matek et al., 2015

claim: The plectonemic structure of DNA can be influenced by the sequence.
source: Various indications that the plectonemic structure of DNA can be influenced by the sequence were obtained from biochemical and structural studies (Kremer et al., 1993; Laundon and Griffith, 1988; Pfannschmidt and Langowski, 1998; Tsen and Levene, 1997) as well as from work performed in silico (Eslami-Mossallam et al., 2016; Pasi and Lavery, 2016; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kremer et al., 1993; Laundon and Griffith, 1988; Pfannschmidt and Langowski, 1998; Tsen and Levene, 1997; Eslami-Mossallam et al., 2016; Pasi and Lavery, 2016; Wang et al., 2017

claim: Plectonemes may get localized to highly curved or flexible segments of DNA.
source: These studies suggested that plectonemes may get localized to highly curved or flexible segments of DNA.
evidence: Inferred from previous studies mentioned in the text

claim: Plectonemes are directly observable as intensity maxima along the DNA in the ISD assay.
source: Plectonemes are directly observable as intensity maxima along the DNA, from which their position along DNA can be extracted (see Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: There is a strong relationship between sequence and plectoneme localization.
source: We find a strong relationship between sequence and plectoneme localization.
evidence: Based on experimental observations described in the manuscript

claim: The local intrinsic curvature determines the relative plectoneme stability at different sequences.
source: Using a model built on basic physics, we show that the local intrinsic curvature determines the relative plectoneme stability at different sequences.
evidence: Based on the physical model developed in the study

claim: Plectonemes localize directly upstream of promoters in prokaryotic genomes.
source: Analysis of several prokaryotic genomes indicates that plectonemes localize directly upstream of promoters, which we experimentally confirm for selected promotor sequences.
evidence: Based on genome analysis and experimental confirmation

claim: Dynamic spots observed along supercoiled DNA molecules are plectonemes induced by supercoiling.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Ganji et al., 2016b; van Loenhout et al., 2012), we observed dynamic spots along the supercoiled DNA molecule (highlighted with arrows in Figure 1b-top left and Video 1). These spots disappeared when DNA torsionally relaxed upon photo-induced nicking (Figure 1b-bottom left) (Ganji et al., 2016b), confirming that the spots were plectonemes induced by the supercoiling.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and citations to Ganji et al., 2016b; van Loenhout et al., 2012

claim: The time-averaged fluorescence intensities of supercoiled DNA are not homogeneously distributed along the molecule.
source: Interestingly, the time-averaged fluorescence intensities of the supercoiled DNA were not homogeneously distributed along the molecule (Figure 1b-top right), establishing that plectoneme occurrence is position dependent.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1b

claim: Torsionally relaxed (nicked) DNA displays a featureless homogenous time-averaged fluorescence intensity.
source: In contrast, torsionally relaxed (nicked) DNA displayed a featureless homogenous time-averaged fluorescence intensity (Figure 1b-bottom right).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1b

claim: Plectoneme positioning is directed by the underlying DNA sequence.
source: Strikingly, the plectoneme densities (Figure 1d) were very different for the two DNA samples. This difference demonstrates that plectoneme positioning is directed by the underlying DNA sequence.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d comparing two different DNA templates

claim: The interaction of dye is not responsible for the position-dependent plectoneme density.
source: Note that we did not observe any position dependence in the intensity profiles when the DNA was torsionally relaxed, indicating that the interaction of dye is not responsible for the dependence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a

claim: The number of nucleation and termination events for plectonemes is position dependent.
source: The plectoneme kinetics showed a similar sequence dependence, as the number of events for nucleation and termination of plectonemes was also found to be position dependent with very different profiles for each DNA samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b

claim: At each position of the DNA, the number of nucleation and termination events are the same, showing that the system is at equilibrium.
source: Importantly, at each position of the DNA, the number of nucleation and termination events were the same, showing that the system was at equilibrium.
evidence: Based on analysis of nucleation and termination events

claim: The plectoneme density shows a weak correlation with the local AT-percentage (R = 0.33).
source: Indeed, the plectoneme density showed a weak correlation with the local AT-percentage (R = 0.33, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a

claim: All three AT-rich inserts (seqA, seqB, and seqC) showed a peak in the plectoneme density at the position of insertion.
source: Interestingly, all three samples showed a peak in the plectoneme density at the position of insertion, further supporting the idea that AT-rich sequences are preferred positions for plectonemes (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: The probability of plectoneme pinning scales with the length of the AT-rich fragment.
source: Furthermore, when we shortened or lengthened one AT-rich sequence (seqA), we found that the probability of plectoneme pinning (i.e. the area under the peak) scaled with the length of the AT-rich fragment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–e

claim: Plectoneme preferentially form at AT-rich regions.
source: Overall, these results suggest that plectoneme preferentially form at AT-rich regions.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results on AT-rich sequences

claim: Removing all poly(A) tracts of length four or higher by replacing alternative A-bases with G or C-bases eliminates the peak in plectoneme density.
source: To test this, we removed all poly(A) tracts of length four or higher by replacing alternative A-bases with G or C-bases in seqCopy (Figure 2c, 'A-G mutation'). Upon this change, the peak in the plectoneme density indeed disappeared (Figure 2d, blue).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c-d

claim: Disrupting poly(A)≥4 tracts by replacing them with alternating AT-stretches still results in strong plectoneme pinning.
source: However, when we instead disrupted the poly(A)≥4 tracts by replacing them with alternating AT-stretches (Figure 2c, 'A-T mutation'), we, surprisingly, did observe strong pinning (Figure 2d, red), establishing that plectoneme pinning does not strictly require poly(A)-tracts either.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c-d

claim: Breaking up all poly(A/T)≥4 tracts by shuffling bases within the seqB insert while keeping the overall AT-content the same eliminates plectoneme-pinning.
source: Here, we broke up all poly(A/T)≥4 tracts (i.e. all linear stretches with a random mixture of A or T bases but no G or C bases) by shuffling bases within the seqB insert while keeping the overall AT-content the same. This eliminated plectoneme-pinning, consistent with the idea that poly(A/T) tracts were the cause (Figure 2e–f, purple).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e-f

claim: Keeping all poly(A/T)≥4 tracts intact but rearranging their positions within the seqB insert abolishes the pinning pattern.
source: However, if we instead kept all poly(A/T)≥4 tracts intact, but merely rearranged their positions within the seqB insert (again keeping AT-content the same), this rearrangement abolished the pinning pattern (Figure 2f, orange), indicating that plectoneme pinning is not solely dependent on the presence of poly(A/T) stretches, but instead is dependent on the relative positions of these stretches.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f

claim: Plectoneme pinning depends on a local mechanical property arising from the combined effect of the entire base sequences in a local region.
source: Our data instead suggest that plectoneme pinning depends on a local mechanical property arising from the combined effect of the entire base sequences in a local region, and our shuffled poly(A/T) constructs suggest this property must be measured over distances greater than tens of nucleotides.
evidence: Inferred from systematic experimental exploration of various sequences

claim: Duplex stability is unlikely to be a determinant factor for plectoneme pinning because it is mostly determined by the overall AT/GC percentage rather than the specific distribution of bases in the local region.
source: Among the three mechanical properties we first considered, duplex stability, flexibility, and curvature, the duplex stability is unlikely to be a determinant factor for the plectoneme pinning because duplex stability is mostly determined by the overall AT/GC percentage rather than the specific distribution of bases in the local region.
evidence: Based on reasoning about DNA mechanical properties

claim: The major energy cost for making a plectoneme is spent in inducing a strong bend within the DNA in the plectoneme tip region.
source: Notably, the major energy cost for making a plectoneme is spent in inducing a strong bend within the DNA in the plectoneme tip region.
evidence: Based on physical modeling of plectoneme formation

claim: At 3pN of tension, the estimated size of the bent tip is 73 bp, and the energy required to bend it by 240° is approximately 18 kBT.
source: For example, at 3pN of tension (characteristic for our stretched DNA molecules), the estimated size of the bent tip is 73 bp, and the energy required to bend it by 240° is very sizeable,~18 kBT (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: Based on physical model calculations shown in Figure 3a-b

claim: An intrinsic curvature of 60˚ between the two ends of a 73 bp segment would lower the bending energy by approximately 8 kBT.
source: For example, an intrinsic curvature of 60˚ between the two ends of a 73 bp segment would lower the bending energy by a sizable amount,~8 kBT.
evidence: Based on physical model calculations

claim: The predicted energy landscape for plectoneme formation is rough with a standard deviation of about ~1 kBT.
source: The predicted energy landscape is found to be rough with a standard deviation of about ~1 kBT, in agreement with a previous experimental estimate based on plectoneme diffusion rates (van Loenhout et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on model predictions and citation to van Loenhout et al., 2012

claim: The model predicts that flexibility is unimportant and that intrinsic curvature is the dominant factor in positioning plectonemes.
source: Although both intrinsic curvature and flexibility were included, the model predicts that the flexibility is unimportant and that intrinsic curvature clearly is the dominant factor in positioning plectonemes (Figure 3c).
evidence: Based on model predictions shown in Figure 3c

claim: The predicted plectoneme densities are generally in very good agreement with the measured plectoneme densities.
source: The predicted plectoneme densities (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) are generally found to be in very good agreement with the measured plectoneme densities.
evidence: Based on comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The model qualitatively represents the experimental data for the large majority of the sequences that were tested.
source: More generally, we find that the model qualitatively represented the experimental data for the large majority of the sequences that were tested (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The model is too conservative, performing well in avoiding false positives but suffering from some false negatives.
source: Only occasionally, we find that the model is too conservative, that is while it performs well in avoiding false positives, it suffers from some false negatives (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, SeqA, SeqB, and SeqC), possibly because of an insufficient accuracy in the dinucleotide parameters that we adopted from the literature.
evidence: Based on comparison of model predictions with experimental data

claim: Different dinucleotide parameter sets from the currently available literature produce variations in the model predictions.
source: For example, different dinucleotide parameter sets from the currently available literature produce variations in the model predictions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on model predictions using different parameter sets shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: A 250 bp-long sequence designed to have high local curvature shows strong plectoneme pinning.
source: As a test of the predictive power of our model, we designed a 250 bp-long sequence ('curved250') for which our model a priori predicted a high local curvature and strong plectoneme pinning (Figure 3e). When we subsequently synthesized and measured this construct, we indeed observed a pronounced peak in the plectoneme density (Figure 3f, blue).
evidence: Based on model prediction and experimental validation shown in Figure 3e-f

claim: A 500 bp-long flat sequence without strongly curved regions shows no plectoneme pinning peak.
source: By contrast, when we constructed a 500 bp-long flat sequence without strongly curved regions ('flat500'), the model predicted no such peak, which again was verified experimentally (Figure 3f, black).
evidence: Based on model prediction and experimental validation shown in Figure 3f

claim: A single highly curved DNA sequence of only 75 bp length is able to pin plectonemes.
source: Perhaps most strikingly, we found that a single highly curved DNA sequence of only 75 bp length was able to pin plectonemes (Figure 3g), consistent with the approximated tip loop size in our physical model (~73 bp).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3g

claim: A 75 bp-long flat DNA sequence does not show plectoneme pinning.
source: As a negative control, we did not observe any such pinning when we inserted a 75 bp-long flat DNA sequence (Figure 3h).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3h

claim: GC-rich curved sequences can pin plectonemes.
source: As predicted by the model, the experimental data for this GC-rich curved sequence showed plectoneme pinning (Figure 3i), once more confirming that intrinsic curvature and not AT/GC content is the major determinant for plectoneme pinning.
evidence: Based on model prediction and experimental validation shown in Figure 3i

claim: Intrinsic curvature and not AT/GC content is the major determinant for plectoneme pinning.
source: As predicted by the model, the experimental data for this GC-rich curved sequence showed plectoneme pinning (Figure 3i), once more confirming that intrinsic curvature and not AT/GC content is the major determinant for plectoneme pinning.
evidence: Based on experimental validation of GC-rich curved sequences

claim: In prokaryotes, curved DNA has been observed to localize upstream of transcription start sites (TSS).
source: For example, in prokaryotes, curved DNA has been observed to localize upstream of transcription start sites (TSS) (Kanhere and Bansal, 2005; Olivares-Zavaleta et al., 2006; Pérez-Martín et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kanhere and Bansal, 2005; Olivares-Zavaleta et al., 2006; Pérez-Martín et al., 1994

claim: In eukaryotes, curvature is associated with the nucleosome positioning sequences found near promoters.
source: In eukaryotes, curvature is associated with the nucleosome positioning sequences found near promoters (Tompitak et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tompitak et al., 2017

claim: A substantial fraction of plectonemic hot spots in the E. coli genome are localized ~100 nucleotides upstream of all the transcription start sites (TSS).
source: Interestingly, we find that a substantial fraction of these hot spots are localized ~100 nucleotides upstream of all the transcription start sites (TSS) associated with confirmed genes in the RegulonDB database (Figure 4b, red) (Gama-Castro et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on genome analysis shown in Figure 4b and citation to Gama-Castro et al., 2016

claim: A peak upstream of the TSS is consistently observed in several prokaryotic genomes, but the size of the peak varies substantially between species.
source: We consistently observe a peak upstream of the TSS, but the size of the peak varied substantially between species, indicating that different organisms rely on sequence-dependent plectoneme positioning to different extents.
evidence: Based on analysis of several prokaryotic genomes

claim: In C. crescentus, the plectoneme positioning signal upstream of TSS was too weak to detect.
source: In one organism (C. crescentus), the signal was too weak to detect at all.
evidence: Based on genome analysis

claim: Two putative plectoneme-pinning sites from E. coli (TSS-rrsB and TSS-polA) show strong pinning effect in the single-molecule assay.
source: To experimentally confirm that these sequences represent plectonemic hot spots, we inserted two of these putative plectoneme-pinning sites from E. coli into template1. Gratifyingly, we indeed observed a strong pinning effect for these sequences in our single-molecule assay (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: Based on experimental validation shown in Figure 4c-d

claim: Most eukaryotic organisms show both peaks and valleys in plectoneme density around the promoter, indicating plectonemes are enriched but also depleted at different regions.
source: While one organism (S. cervisiae) showed no detectable plectoneme positioning, most organisms showed both peaks and valleys indicating plectonemes were enriched but also depleted at different regions around the promoter.
evidence: Based on genome analysis shown in Figure 4f

claim: The features of plectoneme density around eukaryotic promoters show a weak periodicity consistent with the reported nucleosome repeat lengths (~150–260 bp).
source: The features showed a weak periodicity consistent with the reported nucleosome repeat lengths (~150–260 bp) (Jiang and Pugh, 2009).
evidence: Based on genome analysis and citation to Jiang and Pugh, 2009

claim: Intrinsic curvature over a ~ 70 bp range is the primary factor that determines plectoneme pinning in the positive supercoiling regime.
source: In the positive supercoiling regime (where no partial duplex melting is expected for the physiological range of tensions and torques), we identified the intrinsic curvature over a ~ 70 bp range as the primary factor that determines plectoneme pinning, while the flexibility alters the mechanics only minimally.
evidence: Based on physical modeling and experimental validation

claim: Plectonemes are enriched at promoter sequences in E. coli and other prokaryotes.
source: Examining full genomes, we found that plectonemes are enriched at promoter sequences in E. coli and other prokaryotes, which suggests a role of genetically encoded supercoils in cellular function.
evidence: Based on genome analysis

claim: A 'hidden code' of intrinsic curvature governs the localization of local DNA supercoils and the organization of the three-dimensional structure of the genome.
source: Our findings reveal how a previously unrecognized 'hidden code' of intrinsic curvature governs the localization of local DNA supercoils, and hence the organization of the three-dimensional structure of the genome.
evidence: Based on the overall findings of the study

claim: Highly flexible mismatched single-stranded regions can act as a preferential position for plectoneme formation.
source: Although highly flexible mismatched single-stranded regions have been shown to be able to act as a preferential position for plectoneme formation (Dittmore et al., 2017; Ganji et al., 2016b), the variations in the flexibility of duplex DNA due to sequence differences seem to produce very minor changes in the pinning probability.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dittmore et al., 2017; Ganji et al., 2016b

claim: Variations in the flexibility of duplex DNA due to sequence differences produce very minor changes in the pinning probability.
source: Although highly flexible mismatched single-stranded regions have been shown to be able to act as a preferential position for plectoneme formation (Dittmore et al., 2017; Ganji et al., 2016b), the variations in the flexibility of duplex DNA due to sequence differences seem to produce very minor changes in the pinning probability.
evidence: Based on the findings of the study

claim: Curved DNA upstream to the promoter site affects gene expression levels in vivo.
source: Moreover, early in vivo studies showed that curved DNA upstream to the promoter site affects gene expression levels (Collis et al., 1989; McAllister and Achberger, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Collis et al., 1989; McAllister and Achberger, 1989

claim: Curved DNA facilitates binding of RNA polymerase.
source: These in vivo studies suggested that curved DNA facilitates binding of RNA polymerase, an idea that is further supported by sharply bent DNA structures found around bound RNAP (Rees et al., 1993; Tahirov et al., 2002; ten Heggeler and Wahli, 1985; Yin and Steitz, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rees et al., 1993; Tahirov et al., 2002; ten Heggeler and Wahli, 1985; Yin and Steitz, 2002

claim: Curved DNA can pin a plectoneme that can regulate transcription initiation and elongation by structural re-arrangement of the promotor and coding regions.
source: In addition to this direct interaction of RNA polymerase and curved DNA, our results suggest an indirect effect, as the same curved DNA can easily pin a plectoneme that can further regulate the transcription initiation and elongation by structural re-arrangement of the promotor and coding regions.
evidence: Based on the findings of the study

claim: Promoter sequences have evolved local regions with highly curved DNA that promote the localization of DNA plectonemes at these sites.
source: Our analysis of prokaryotic genomes indicates that promoter sequences have evolved local regions with highly curved DNA that promote the localization of DNA plectonemes at these sites.
evidence: Based on genome analysis

claim: Plectonemes may help to expose DNA regions to the outer edge of the dense nucleoid, making them accessible to RNAP, transcription factors, and topoisomerases.
source: For one, it may help to expose these DNA regions to the outer edge of the dense nucleoid, making them accessible to RNAP, transcription factors, and topoisomerases.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the biological role of plectonemes

claim: Plectonemes may play a role in the bursting dynamics of gene expression.
source: Plectonemes may also play a role in the bursting dynamics of gene expression, since each RNAP alters the supercoiling density within a topological domain as it transcribes (Chong et al., 2014; Kouzine et al., 2013), adding or removing nearby plectonemes (Liu and Wang, 1987).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to Chong et al., 2014; Kouzine et al., 2013; Liu and Wang, 1987

claim: By bringing distant regions of DNA close together, plectonemes may influence specific promoter-enhancer interactions to regulate gene expression.
source: In addition, by bringing distant regions of DNA close together, plectonemes may influence specific promoter-enhancer interactions to regulate gene expression (Benedetti et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citation to Benedetti et al., 2014

claim: Plectoneme tips may help RNA polymerase to initiate transcription, since the formation of an open complex also requires bending of the DNA.
source: Finally, plectoneme tips may help RNA polymerase to initiate transcription, since the formation of an open complex also requires bending of the DNA (ten Heggeler-Bordier et al., 1992), a mechanism that was proposed as a universal method of regulating gene expression across all organisms (Travers and Muskhelishvili, 2007).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to ten Heggeler-Bordier et al., 1992; Travers and Muskhelishvili, 2007

claim: Plectonemes may play a role in positioning nucleosomes in eukaryotes.
source: The spacing of the peaks suggests that plectonemes may play a role in positioning nucleosomes, consistent with proposals that nucleosome positioning may rely on sequence-dependent signals near promoters (Travers et al., 2010).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citation to Travers et al., 2010

claim: The plectoneme signal encoded by intrinsic curvature could indirectly position the promoter plectoneme tip by helping to organize nearby nucleosomes in eukaryotes.
source: The plectoneme signal encoded by intrinsic curvature could therefore indirectly position the promoter plectoneme tip by helping to organize these nearby nucleosomes.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on genome analysis

claim: For negative supercoils, plectoneme pinning can be influenced by both sequence-induced local curvature and local melting.
source: For negative supercoils, plectoneme pinning can be influenced by both sequence-induced local curvature and local melting, which are hard to disentangle.
evidence: Based on reasoning about negative supercoiling

claim: The model developed for positive supercoils should not be very sensitive to the handedness of supercoiling and is expected to capture curvature-dependent effects on pinning of negative plectonemes.
source: The model that we have developed for positive supercoils should not be very sensitive to the handedness of supercoiling, since the dinucleotide curvature parameters are not strongly perturbed at these torques. We therefore expect the model to also capture curvature-dependent effects on pinning of negative plectonemes too.
evidence: Based on reasoning about the model's applicability

claim: DNA contains a previously hidden 'code' that determines the local intrinsic curvature and consequently governs the locations of plectonemes.
source: The above findings demonstrate that DNA contains a previously hidden 'code' that determines the local intrinsic curvature and consequently governs the locations of plectonemes.
evidence: Based on the overall findings of the study

claim: Plectonemes can organize DNA within topological domains, providing fine-scale control of the three-dimensional structure of the genome.
source: These plectonemes can organize DNA within topological domains, providing fine-scale control of the three-dimensional structure of the genome (Le et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on the findings of the study and citation to Le et al., 2013

claim: SxO does not have any considerable effect on the mechanical properties of DNA under the experimental conditions used.
source: Notably, SxO does not have any considerable effect on the mechanical properties of DNA under our experimental conditions (Ganji et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ganji et al., 2016b

claim: Each intercalating dye (SxO) is bound on approximately every 26 base-pairs of DNA.
source: Based on the same previous work and assuming that each intercalating dye reduces the twist at the local dinucleotide to zero, we estimate that roughly 1 SxO is bound on every 26 base-pairs of DNA.
evidence: Based on estimation from previous work

claim: Increasing the NaCl concentration from 20 mM to 150 mM NaCl does not result in any significant difference in the observed plectoneme density results.
source: Furthermore, we verified that increasing the NaCl concentration from 20 mM to 150 mM NaCl did not result in any significant difference in the observed plectoneme density results, indicating that the plectoneme density is not dependent on the ionic strength (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f

claim: The plectoneme density is not dependent on the ionic strength.
source: Furthermore, we verified that increasing the NaCl concentration from 20 mM to 150 mM NaCl did not result in any significant difference in the observed plectoneme density results, indicating that the plectoneme density is not dependent on the ionic strength (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f

claim: The parameter set by Balasubramanian et al. produces the closest match to experimental data when plugged into the model.
source: We find that the parameter set by Balasubramanian et al., produces the closest match to our experimental data when plugged into our model (Balasubramanian et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on comparison of model predictions using different parameter sets with experimental data
